'''Susan Solomon''' (born 1956) is an American atmospheric chemist, working for most of her career at the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA).<ref name="NAS">{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/susan-solomon.html|title=InterViews|access-date=February 17, 2013|date=July 26, 2004|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210203810/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/susan-solomon.html|archive-date=February 10, 2015|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref> In 2011, Solomon joined the faculty at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where she serves as the [[Ellen Swallow Richards]] Professor of Atmospheric Chemistry & Climate Science.<ref>{{cite web|title=People|work=Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences website|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|url=https://eapsweb.mit.edu/people/solos|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref> Solomon, with her colleagues, was the first to propose the [[chlorofluorocarbon]] [[free radical]] [[reaction mechanism]] that is the cause of the Antarctic [[ozone hole]].<ref name="NAS"/> Her most recent book, ''Solvable: how we healed the earth, and how we can do it again'' (2024) focuses on solutions to current problems, as do books by data scientist [[Hannah Ritchie]], marine biologist, [[Ayana Elizabeth Johnson]] and climate scientist [[Katharine Hayhoe]].<ref name="Buckley"/>

Solomon is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences|U.S. National Academy of Sciences]], the European Academy of Sciences, and the [[French Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Top">{{cite web|url=https://celebrating200years.noaa.gov/historymakers/solomon/welcome.html|title=Susan Solomon: Pioneering Atmospheric Scientist|date=January 5, 2007|work=Top Tens: History Makers|publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
In 2002, ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized her  as one of the 50 most important women in science.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite news|last1=Svitil|first1=Kathy|title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science|url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/the-50-most-important-women-in-science|access-date=31 January 2023|publisher=Discover|date=13 November 2002}}</ref>
In 2008, Solomon was selected by ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine as one of the 100 most influential people in the world.<ref>"[https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/completelist/0,29569,1733748,00.html The 2008 TIME 100]", ''Time''.</ref> She also serves on the Science and Security Board for the [[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thebulletin.org/about-us/science-and-security-board/|title=Science and Security Board|website=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>

==Biography==
[[File:Susan Solomon crop 2010 Ullyot Public Affairs Lecture.jpg|thumb|Susan Solomon, 2010|alt=|left]]

===Early life===
Solomon was born in Chicago, Illinois.<ref name="WIC">{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/susan-solomon|access-date=February 6, 2019|title=Susan Solomon|website=Science History Institute|date=June 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/solomon-susan-1956|title=Solomon, Susan (1956– ) {{!}} Encyclopedia.com|website=www.encyclopedia.com|access-date=2020-02-21}}</ref> Her interest in science began as a child watching ''[[The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau]]''.<ref name="WIC"/> In high school she placed third in a national science competition, with a project that measured the percentage of oxygen in a gas mixture.<ref name="WIC"/>

Solomon received a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in [[chemistry]] from the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] in 1977.  She then received an [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in chemistry in 1979 followed by a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1981 in [[atmospheric chemistry]], both from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="NAS"/>

===Personal life===
Solomon married Barry Sidwell in 1988.<ref>{{cite book|author=Oakes, Elizabeth H.|title=Encyclopedia of world scientists|year=2007|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=9781438118826|page=679|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA679}}</ref> She is Jewish.<ref>{{Cite web|title=MIT's Jewish environmental warrior: 'Earth has a budget'|url=https://www.jpost.com/50-most-influential-jews/susan-solomon-678152|access-date=2022-01-06|website=The Jerusalem Post |date=September 12, 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Work===
Solomon was the head of the Chemistry and Climate Processes Group of the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] Chemical Sciences Division until 2011. In 2011, she joined the faculty of the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.<ref>{{cite news|author=Krajick, Kevin|title=Two Climate Scientists Win 2012 Vetlesen Prize for Work on Ozone Hole, Ice Cores|url=http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/news-events/two-climate-scientists-win-vetlesen-prize-work-ozone-hole-ice-cores|website=Lamont -Doherty Earth Observatory|date=January 14, 2013|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>

* ''The Coldest March: Scott's Fatal Antarctic Expedition'',<ref name="Solomon">{{cite book
 | last = Solomon
 | first = S.
 | author-link = Susan Solomon
 | year = 2001

 | publisher = [[Yale University Press]]
 | location = London

 | url-access = registration

 }}</ref> Yale University Press, 2002 {{ISBN|0-300-09921-5}} – Depicts the tale of Captain [[Robert Falcon Scott]]'s failed 1912 [[Antarctic]] expedition, specifically applying the comparison of modern meteorological data with that recorded by Scott's expedition in an attempt to shed new light on the reasons for the demise of Scott's polar party.<ref>{{cite news|author=MacFarlane, Robert|title=In from the cold...|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2001/oct/07/historybooks.highereducation|work=[[The Observer]]|date=October 7, 2001|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Wheeler, Sara|title=Great Scott?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/02/books/great-scott.html|access-date=February 6, 2019|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=September 2, 2001}}</ref>
* ''Aeronomy of the Middle Atmosphere: Chemistry and Physics of the Stratosphere and Mesosphere'', 3rd Edition, Springer, 2005 {{ISBN|1-4020-3284-6}} – Describes the atmospheric chemistry and physics of the middle atmosphere from {{convert|10|to|100|km}} altitude.<ref name="Brasseur">{{cite book|author1=Brasseur, Guy|author2=Solomon, Susan|title=Aeronomy of the middle atmosphere: chemistry and physics of the stratosphere and mesosphere|year=2005|publisher=Springer|location=Dordrecht|isbn=1-4020-3284-6|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z5OtlDjfXkkC&pg=PA1}}</ref>
* {{cite book |last1=Solomon |first1=Susan |title=Solvable: how we healed the earth, and how we can do it again |date=2024 |publisher=The University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago; London |isbn=9780226827933}}<ref name="Buckley">{{cite news |last1=Buckley |first1=Cara |title=Solving Problems With Susan Solomon |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/18/climate/susan-solomon-q-and-a.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=18 July 2024 |work=The New York Times |date=18 July 2024}}</ref>

====The Ozone Hole====
Solomon, working with colleagues at the NOAA [[Earth System Research Laboratories]], postulated the mechanism that the Antarctic ozone hole was created by a [[heterogeneous reaction]] of ozone and chlorofluorocarbons free radicals on the surface of ice particles in the high altitude clouds that form over Antarctica. In 1986 and 1987 Solomon led the National Ozone Expedition to [[McMurdo Sound]], where the team gathered the evidence to confirm the accelerated reactions.<ref name="NAS"/> Solomon was the solo leader of the expedition, and the only woman on the team.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Indivero, Victoria M.|title=Changing views on climate|journal=Chemical Heritage Magazine|date=Fall 2010|volume=28|issue=3|page=13|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/changing-views-on-climate}}</ref> Her team measured levels of [[chlorine oxide]] 100 times higher than expected in the atmosphere, which had been released by the decomposition of chlorofluorocarbons by [[ultraviolet radiation]].<ref name="Nickel">{{cite web|author=Nickel, Mark|title=Brown confers six honorary degrees|url=https://news.brown.edu/articles/2015/04/honoraries|website=Brown University|date=April 28, 2015|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>

Solomon later showed that [[volcanoes]] could accelerate the reactions caused by [[chlorofluorocarbon]]s, and so increase the damage to the ozone layer. Her work formed the basis of the U.N. [[Montreal Protocol]], an international agreement to protect the ozone layer by regulating damaging chemicals.<ref name="WIC"/><ref>{{cite news|author=Daley, Megan|title=Decades after the Montreal Protocol, there are signs the hole in the ozone layer has begun to heal|url=http://www.latimes.com/projects/la-sci-sn-ozone-hole-healing/|access-date=February 6, 2019|work=Los Angeles Times|date=June 30, 2016}}</ref> Solomon has also presented some research which suggests that implementation of the Montreal Protocols is having a positive effect.<ref>{{cite news|title=Ozone layer on the mend thirty years after CFCs banned|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/environment/ozone-layer-on-the-mend-thirty-years-after-cfcs-banned-1.2706793|access-date=February 6, 2019|work=[[Irish Times]]|date=July 1, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Solomon, S.|author2=Ivy, D. J.|author3=Kinnison, D.|author4=Mills, M. J.|author5=Neely, R. R.|author6=Schmidt, A.|title=Emergence of healing in the Antarctic ozone layer|journal=Science|date=July 15, 2016|volume=353|issue=6296|pages=269–274|doi=10.1126/science.aae0061|bibcode=2016Sci...353..269S|pmid=27365314|doi-access=free|hdl=1721.1/107197|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

For her critical contribution to saving the ozone layer, Solomon was a winner of the 2021 Future of Life Award along with Joe Farman and Stephen O. Andersen.  Jim Hansen, former Director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Director of Columbia University's Program on Climate Science, Awareness and Solutions said, "In Farman, Solomon and Andersen we see the tremendous impact individuals can have not only on the course of human history, but on the course of our planet's history. My hope is that others like them will emerge in today's battle against climate change."<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=Future Of Life Award|url=https://futureoflife.org/future-of-life-award/|access-date=2021-09-27|website=Future of Life Institute|language=en-US}}</ref> Professor Guus Velders, a climate scientist at Utrecht University said, "Susan Solomon is a deserving recipient of the Future of Life Award. Susan not only explained the processes behind the formation of the ozone hole, she also played an active role as an interface between the science and policy of the Montreal Protocol."<ref name="auto"/>

====''The Coldest March''====
Using research work conducted by English explorer and navy officer [[Robert Falcon Scott]], Solomon also wrote and spoke about Scott's 1911 expedition in ''The Coldest March: Scott's Fatal Antarctic Expedition''<ref name="Solomon" /> to counter a longstanding argument that blamed Scott for his and his crew's demise during that expedition. Scott attributed his death to unforeseen weather conditions – a claim that has been contested by British journalist and author [[Roland Huntford]]. Huntford claimed that Scott was a prideful and under-prepared leader. Solomon has defended  Scott and said that "modern data side squarely with Scott", describing the weather conditions in 1911 as unusual.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Monastersky, Richard|date=September 7, 2001|title=History's Cold Shoulder|journal=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]]|pages=A20}}</ref>

====Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change====
Solomon served on the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]].<ref name="NAS"/> She was a contributing author for the [[IPCC Third Assessment Report|Third Assessment Report]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Houghton, J.T.|title=Climate Change 2001: The Scientific Basis|work=Third Assessment Report|publisher=Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|year=2001|page=21|url=https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_995493/component/file_995492/content|access-date=February 6, 2019|display-authors=etal}}</ref> She was also co-chair of Working Group I for the [[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report|Fourth Assessment Report]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Herbert, Betsy|title=Climate Change 2007 The Physical Science Basis|work=Fourth Assessment Report|publisher=Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|year=2007|url=http://www.slvwd.com/agendas/Full/2007/06-07-07/Item%2010b.pdf|access-date=February 6, 2019|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

* 1994 – [[Solomon Saddle]] ({{coord|78|23|S|162|39|E|display=inline}}), a snow saddle at about {{convert|1850|m|ft|-1}} elevation, named in her honor
* 1994 – [[Solomon Glacier]] ({{coord|78|23|S|162|30|E|display=inline}}), an Antarctic glacier named in her honor
* 1999 – [[National Medal of Science]], awarded by the [[President of the United States]]<ref>{{cite web|title=1999 National Medals of Science and Technology|work=[[Scientific American]]|publisher=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/1999-national-medals-of-s/|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
* 2000 – [[Carl-Gustaf Rossby Research Medal]], awarded by the [[American Meteorological Society]]<ref name="AMS">{{cite web|title=AMS Awards and Nomination Information|publisher=American Meteorological Society|url=http://www.ametsoc.org/awards/index.html|access-date=March 8, 2013}}</ref>
* 2004 – [[Blue Planet Prize]],  awarded by the Asahi Glass Foundation<ref>{{cite web|title=Blue Planet Prize: The Laureates|work=Blue Plant Prize website|publisher=Asahi Glass Foundation|url=http://www.af-info.or.jp/en/blueplanet/list.html|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
* 2006 – [[V. M. Goldschmidt Award]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.geochemsoc.org/honors/awards/vmgoldschmidtaward|title=V. M. Goldschmidt Award|publisher=Geochemical Society|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>

* 2007 – [[William Bowie Medal]], awarded by the [[American Geophysical Union]]<ref>{{cite news|publisher=[[Earth System Research Laboratories]]|url=https://www.esrl.noaa.gov/csd/news/2007/36_0716.html|title=Susan Solomon Honored as AGU's 2007 William Bowie Medalist|date=July 16, 2007|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
* 2007 — [[Prix Georges Lemaître]]

* 2008 – [[Grande Médaille]] (Great Medal) of the French Academy of Sciences<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.academie-sciences.fr/archivage_site/activite/prix/s241108_hoffmann_solomon.pdf|title=Remise de la Grande Médaille par Jules Hoffmann, Président de l'Académie,à Susan Solomon|date=November 25, 2008|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
* 2008 – Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Susan Solomon |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/susan-solomon-12317/ |website=Royal Society |access-date=24 November 2020}}</ref>
*2008 – Member of the [[American Philosophical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Susan+Solomon&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-04-28|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>

Heyman Service to America Medals|Service to America Medal]], awarded by the [[Partnership for Public Service]]<ref>{{cite web|title=2010 Career Achievement Medal Recipient|work=Service to America Medals website|publisher=Partnership for Public Service|year=2010|url=https://www.esrl.noaa.gov/news/2010/ESRLs_Susan_Solomon_Wins_Service_to_America_Medal.html|access-date=February 6, 2019}}</ref>
